cards.title: Define brand ideals before choosing visual solutions
cards.summary: Use a shared set of ten brand ideals to align decisions before designers show concepts, whether you launch, reposition or extend.
cards.use_when: Approving or rejecting a logo/identity concept, refreshing packaging, or briefing any designer for a new product line or store rebrand.
steps: Write down how the business scores on the ten ideals named in the source: vision, meaning, authenticity, differentiation, sustainability, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, and design excellence.
Rate where you are strong and weak on each. The source treats brand identity as a strategic asset, so gaps here become constraints on any visual work.
Treat design excellence as a given rather than a differentiator; the source argues the best brands marry intelligence and insight with imagination and craft, not just a nice look.
Use this list as the brief you hand to designers and the scorecard you use when evaluating concepts, so you judge proposals against brand logic instead of personal taste.
Revisit the ideals when you launch, reposition, merge or add a retail presence; the source states they hold across all these engagements.
caveats: These are the source's ideals, not a validated scoring model with numeric benchmarks.
Small brands can adopt them, but the source gives no evidence about cost or timing for tiny teams.

cards.title: Use functional criteria as the minimum bar for any mark
cards.summary: Check any proposed mark or logo against nine functional criteria before approving it, because aesthetics alone do not make a usable identity.
cards.use_when: Selecting a logo for a new store, product label, packaging or app icon, or auditing an existing mark that may be failing on small screens.
steps: Test the proposed mark against the source's functional criteria: bold, memorable and appropriate; immediately recognizable; a consistent image of the company; clearly communicating the company persona; legally protectable; enduring value; works across media and scale; and works in both black and white and color.
Physically preview the mark at the sizes your store uses: favicon, packaging panel, label, mobile icon and signage. The source notes identity must work at every scale.
Check trademark availability with an IP professional before committing, since the source treats legal protection as a functional requirement rather than an afterthought.
Run the mark in single color and full color before launch; the source lists this as a criterion, so a mark that only works in color is not finished.
Forget nothing: ask whether the mark still reads as your brand when seen out of context.
caveats: The source does not rank criteria or explain which trade-offs to make when criteria conflict.
Legal protectability generally requires advice from a trademark attorney, not the designer alone.

cards.title: Write meaning before visuals so approval stops being a taste fight
cards.summary: Establish a written framework of meaning for the identity so decision-makers agree on brand essence and attributes before any visual solutions are presented.
cards.use_when: Running a rebrand, product-line identity, or packaging redesign where stakeholders keep disagreeing on subjective grounds.
steps: Document what the brand stands for—the big idea, strategic position, values and voice—before showing logo options, naming options or key messages.
Use that written framework as the rallying point for decision-makers; the source compares meaning to a campfire that builds consensus and precedes any presentation of visual solutions.
Require every element in the identity system to have a rationale within that framework, so each choice can be explained, understood, communicated and approved.
Expect meaning to evolve as the business changes; plan to revisit the written framework when the assortment, business model or market shifts.
When a concept is rejected, go back to the framework rather than iterating blindly on visuals.
caveats: The source is a general brand-identity framework, not empirical evidence that written frameworks improve outcomes.
Meaning that evolves over time requires periodic review, which adds process overhead.

cards.title: Distill the brand name into its meanings
cards.summary: Take each word or part of the brand name and explore it as different parts of speech to surface nuances and unify the team around key messages.
cards.use_when: Naming a private label, a new product line or a sub-brand, or choosing taglines and messaging for a landing page.
steps: Write the proposed name or a long scientific or descriptive name and split it into each word or component.
Put each component into different parts of speech—verb, adjective, adverb, noun—and note what new meanings and associations emerge.
Use the exercise as a group activity with the client or team; the source's stated purpose is discovery, exploring meaning and nuance and coming together around key messages.
Shortlist the resulting language for taglines, product names, key messages and site copy, then test each on real customer language.

Keep the strongest two or three meanings as your key messages; the source notes that people at risk can comprehend only three messages, and applies the same discipline to brand communications and press relations.
caveats: This is a discovery and alignment exercise from a brand consultancy; it does not predict purchase behavior by itself.
Culturally loaded names need dialect and market checks before adoption.

cards.title: Build coherence across every customer touchpoint
cards.summary: Achieve coherence through one consistent voice, one company strategy and uniform quality rather than rigid rulebooks.
cards.use_when: Auditing the customer experience across product pages, emails, packaging, service replies and checkout, or onboarding new team members who write and design for the brand.
steps: State the positioning clearly and write down how you want to be perceived; coherence begins with internal clarity, not with visual rules.
Adopt a single consistent voice that evolves from one central dynamic idea, and use it in every communication channel.
Treat each touchpoint as a brand experience, including packaging, invoices, emails, replies and the checkout flow; the source says every touchpoint should be considered a brand experience.
Choose a cohesive visual system: designed color, typeface families and formats that advance immediate recognition.
Hold every product and service to the same high quality level; the source argues anything less than superior quality reduces brand value both consciously and unconsciously.
Keep language clear and naming logical inside your architecture so customers can navigate choices on the site without confusion.
caveats: Coherence in the source is explicitly not rigid or limiting; over-enforcing standards can suppress needed marketing creativity.
The source asserts quality effects but cites no measured results.

cards.title: Start from a clear-eyed self-assessment for authenticity
cards.summary: Authenticity in the source means clarity about your market, positioning, value proposition and competitive difference, and doing what you promise.
cards.use_when: Writing the About page, brand story, sustainability claims or any positioning copy for the store, and reviewing whether claims are defensible.
steps: Answer in writing: who we are, what market we serve, how we are positioned, what value we deliver, and how we differ from named competitors.
Audit all claims on packaging, listings and pages against what you actually deliver. One contributor in the source defines authenticity as doing what you promise, not being who you are.
Correct claims you cannot substantiate, because social networks broadcast brands that do not stand true to their promise, per the source's sustainability discussion.
Let expression stay appropriate to your mission, history, culture, values and personality instead of copying a trend aesthetic.
Repeat the self-assessment when the assortment or business model changes; the source treats self-knowledge as the starting position of strength for identity work.
caveats: The source presents two overlapping definitions of authenticity; reconcile them per your context rather than treating either as law.
No method is given for proving consumer perception of authenticity.

cards.title: Design for differentiation that customers can grasp quickly
cards.summary: It is not enough to be different; the source argues brands must demonstrate difference and make it easy for customers to understand.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to present your products against a crowded category on the homepage, PDP or paid creative, or planning a zag when every competitor does the same thing.
steps: Name the category norm explicitly: what does every competitor say and show? Then decide where you will deliberately do something else, per the 'when everybody zigs, zag' guidance in the source.
Translate the difference into a claim a customer can grasp in seconds on a listing, ad or page headline, because the source warns difference alone is not enough.

Reduce choice overload. The source cites the view that best companies curate offerings so consumers are not overwhelmed sorting through every possibility; use this to cut filters, SKUs on a page or bundle options.
Show the difference in product imagery and copy, not just in an adjective; the source says the brand must demonstrate the difference.
Re-test presentation when competitors copy your differentiation, since attention and loyalty are contested by all brands in the category and beyond.
caveats: Curating assortments to reduce overwhelm is a quoted executive opinion in the source, not a tested merchandising rule.
Do not treat differentiation as permission to be confusing; the same passage requires easy understanding.

cards.title: Use flexibility so identity survives new products and interfaces
cards.summary: Build a flexible identity and brand architecture so new products, channels and devices can be added without redesigning the brand each time.
cards.use_when: Planning a logo and identity system for a store that expects new product lines, marketplaces, apps or packaging formats.
steps: Design the identity as a system with parameters rather than a single fixed artwork, so the toolbox allows creativity inside recognizable limits.
Set up a durable brand architecture with an overarching logic for sub-brands, collections and product names, so marketing a new product is facilitated rather than blocked.
Account for unknown future touchpoints. The source notes no one can say with certainty which products or devices will exist in five years, so the system must seize new opportunities quickly.
Test the system on the hardest format you use today, such as a tiny app icon or a mobile page, not only on the largest.
Expect to refresh expression while keeping the central idea; the source describes such design activity as programming and craft dependent, not a one-off set of files.
caveats: Flexibility is not license for inconsistency; the source pairs it with coherence and strict standards.
The source provides no cost or maintenance guidance for flexible systems.

cards.title: Classify your mark to choose the right problem fit
cards.summary: The source groups marks into categories—abstract, pictorial, emblem, letterform, wordmark and signature—and treats the choice as a problem fit, not a rule.
cards.use_when: Briefing a designer or deciding the form of a logo for a store, private label or app icon.
steps: Review the categories against your needs: abstract or symbolic marks carry strategic ambiguity and suit companies with many unrelated divisions; pictorial marks use a literal simplified image; emblems attach the name inextricably to the picture; letterforms use one or more letters as a mnemonic; wordmarks are freestanding names or acronyms.
Note the emblem's specific weakness in the source: as mobile icons and tiny one-sixth-inch logos shrink, emblems present the biggest legibility challenge when miniaturized.
Define the signature, meaning the structured relationship between logotype, brandmark and tagline, and decide whether you need split or horizontal and vertical variations per application.
Choose based on both aspirational and functional criteria, then require a written rationale for the chosen approach.
Combine elements where useful; the source states categories are pliant and many marks combine more than one.
caveats: The source explicitly says there are no hard-and-fast rules for matching a mark type to a company type.
Category boundaries blur, so treat them as a briefing aid rather than a taxonomy.

cards.title: Exploit the shape-then-color-then-form sequence of cognition
cards.summary: Design identity elements around the order in which the brain processes visual information: shape first, color second, language third.
cards.use_when: Choosing a favicon, app icon, packaging panel, ad thumbnail or any visual that must register instantly at small size.
steps: Prioritize a distinctive silhouette, because the source says the brain acknowledges and remembers shapes first and reading is not necessary to identify shapes.
Choose a distinctive color signature second; color can trigger emotion and evoke a brand association, which is why the source notes companies such as Kodak and Tiffany trademarked core colors.
Treat language and wordmarks as third in the sequence, since the brain takes longer to process language; through repeated exposure some companies drop the logotype from advertising entirely.
Apply this to small placements: make the shape work with the color at favicon, icon and thumbnail sizes before adding the name.
Use repeated exposure to build recognition; the source describes color and symbol becoming mnemonic devices when seen frequently.
caveats: The source is a design text describing perception sequence, not a controlled experiment with conversion metrics.
Dropping the logotype depends on very high prior recognition; most young DTC brands cannot assume it.

cards.title: Decide whether a character belongs in your brand
cards.summary: Character trademarks embody brand attributes and can become selling icons, but the source notes they rarely age well and need refreshing.
cards.use_when: Considering a mascot for packaging, kids' products, social content or ad creative, or reviewing whether an existing mascot still fits.
steps: Confirm the character expresses real brand attributes or values rather than being decorative; the source says a character trademark embodies brand attributes or values.
Plan for voice and motion, not just a drawing: the source notes the best characters have recognizable voices and jingles, enabling them to move from shelf to screen.
Budget for periodic redrawing. The source observes that characters rarely age well and usually must be redrawn to stay culturally current, citing Michelin and Betty Crocker as examples.
Test the character for cultural fit in every market you sell in, especially if voices and accents are involved.
Reconsider the mascot when the assortment pivots; a character tied to one product line can become a constraint, as the source illustrates with a former corporate icon tied to a single category.
caveats: Character effectiveness claims in the source are narrative examples, not measured ecommerce results.
Historic characters listed are examples from the source's era and should not be read as recommendations.

cards.title: Build a consistent identity on responsiveness, not separate sites
cards.summary: Use one flexible system with a single content source that adapts across devices instead of designing separate versions for each format.
cards.use_when: Planning the mobile experience of a store, deciding on site architecture, or fixing inconsistent experiences between desktop and mobile shoppers.
steps: Design for the most constrained device first to define parameters, then roll out to larger resolutions, per the fundamentals of responsive design credited in the source to Vijay Mathews.
Establish a clear hierarchy of information that supports an intuitive experience, and structure content access so it responds to the user's environment and behavior, such as on-the-go versus at home.
Keep a clear relationship between resolution families so the site remains visually recognizable across formats.
Account for each device's physical input and build a more native experience, since the source notes not everything is point-and-click.
Use webfonts to preserve legibility across resolutions and formats.
Prefer a singular system with one content management system and a flexible grid over multiple variant sites.
caveats: Responsive design fundamentals are stated as principles; the source gives no measured conversion evidence.
Native input conventions and device families change quickly, so verify current platform guidance.

cards.title: Design icons and apps around one task
cards.summary: The source's stated qualities of the best apps are reliability, compatibility, fast loading, uninterrupted performance and being useful or entertaining, focused on a single task.
cards.use_when: Specifying a store app, a mobile checkout, or an app icon that must compete on a crowded phone home screen.
steps: Pick one task for the app and do it very well; the source states the single easiest way to screw up an app is making it try to do too many things.
Verify the qualities listed: reliable and consistent performance, careful testing, compatibility with the platforms you target, fast loading, and continuous uninterrupted performance.
Design the app icon to express an attribute or brand idea, choosing among iconic, illustrative, photographic, wordmark, letterform or abstract approaches described in the source.
Use color to differentiate a family of apps, as the source describes for one museum's multiple apps, and use letterforms when a single letter already carries your brand equity.
Confirm the icon reads at actual small size, since icons are seen at phone scale rather than presentation scale.
caveats: The qualities list is attributed to a third-party app developer in the source, not to controlled testing.
Performance thresholds and platform interface conventions change; verify current requirements before building.

cards.title: Turn customer experience into video storytelling
cards.summary: The source's video checklist and brand-video uses treat video as a way to express voice, simplify complex subjects and build camaraderie, with the first seconds optimized.
cards.use_when: Briefing a product video, brand film, founder story or channel content plan for a store or marketplace listing.
steps: Optimize the first 15 seconds of the video, per the checklist the source reproduces from a platform creator playbook.

Decide in advance which use the video serves: launching or relaunching a brand with one voice, articulating a common message, simplifying complex subjects by storytelling or animation, or showing personality without reciting a list of attributes.
Include a specific call to action in the video or through annotations and cards.
Set a recurring publishing schedule and build a programming calendar around tentpole events relevant to your audience.
Identify channels with similar content and audiences and create cross-promotion or collaboration videos.
Use analytics on the channel to refine content, programming and production rather than guessing.
caveats: The YouTube checklist is reproduced from a platform document that may have changed; verify current requirements and formats.
Video effectiveness claims in the source are anecdotal, including an internal law-firm example, not ecommerce conversion results.

cards.title: Treat social media as a participative channel with disclosure rules
cards.summary: Follow a five-step social strategy and a disclosure checklist, because consumers are active participants in brand building rather than passive recipients.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing social content, influencer or affiliate programs, and community management for a store.
steps: Define the objective first: customer service, engagement, driving sales or media outreach are different jobs requiring different setups.
Find where your audience is, listen to what they say and build or tap into that community before pushing content.
Plan what you will say; the source warns that a good community with nothing to say cannot sustain conversation.
Decide who manages the activity based on the objective and audience, and invest in training for internal or external people.
Agree metrics in advance and review them regularly, covering outputs, outcomes and impact qualitatively and quantitatively.

Use the disclosure checklist: err on the side of over-disclosure, disclose fully where space allows, hold agencies and contractors to your standards rather than lowering them, and ask whether family and friends or public discussion would make you uncomfortable with the campaign.
caveats: Disclosure norms and platform rules change and vary by market; verify current requirements and legal obligations.
The source debates social ROI and offers no formula.

cards.title: Budget brand work as an asset with legal protection
cards.summary: The source frames brand identity as an intangible asset whose value grows through awareness, recognition, uniqueness and quality, and is preserved through legal protection.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget to branding versus performance, choosing whether to register trademarks, or justifying identity spend to stakeholders.
steps: Treat identity as a strategic business tool that seizes opportunities to build awareness, increase recognition and express competitive difference, rather than a one-off design cost.
Protect the asset: register trademarks and trade dress in the markets you serve, both local and global, and educate employees and vendors about compliance.
Maintain uniform standards and pursue quality relentlessly; the source lists strict adherence as a business priority that preserves value.

Expect value to build through consistent use over time rather than a single campaign, and align the identity with sustainability claims consumers can verify, since the source notes consumers shop their values and social networks expose brands that fail their promise.
Review coverage when you enter new markets or launch new categories, because protection must follow where you sell.
caveats: The source asserts a premium for strong brands but gives no pricing or valuation formula.
Trademark strategy is jurisdiction-specific and needs professional advice.

cards.title: Run the brand like a managed asset with internal tooling
cards.summary: Commitment in the source means active management of brand assets with employee-facing tools; one cited example identifies 101 brand touchpoints organized by country, channel and stakeholder.
cards.use_when: Building brand guidelines, onboarding new employees or agencies, or auditing where your brand shows up across owned channels and packaging.
steps: Inventory your touchpoints, including packaging, emails, listings, invoices, retail or event materials and social profiles; the source's example organizes touchpoints by type, country, channel and stakeholder.
Provide employees with tools that make it easy to be a brand champion, since the source says the best companies supply these rather than relying on policing.
Pair a top-down mandate with bottom-up understanding of why the brand matters, as the source describes for a global brand program.
House best practices in one accessible internal place, using case studies to inform and inspire local implementation rather than only to enforce rules.
Review the touchpoint inventory regularly; the source treats managing the asset as requiring desire and a disciplined approach to keep it relevant.
caveats: The 101-touchpoint figure comes from one large professional-services firm and may not fit a small or mid-sized store.
Internal tooling and content-management systems require ongoing maintenance the source does not budget.

cards.title: Enter complex markets through local partners and naming research
cards.summary: In markets the source describes as most complex, such as China, the most successful companies do not rush and instead build native partnerships and test naming across dialects.
cards.use_when: Launching or expanding a store into a new country or region, or adapting product names and marketing copy for a new market.
steps: Begin by finding in-country native partners and advisors, and take the necessary time to build relationships based on trust, respect and understanding, per the source's account of successful multinationals in China.
Treat naming as the hardest decision: decide whether to blend or balance East and West or emphasize one, and check what the name sounds like and means across dialects.
Commission extensive research before launch, because the source attributes China's branding complexity to diverse regional, linguistic and cultural nuances and relative newness to branding.
Adapt rather than export; the source quotes the view that succeeding in China is adapting to China, and that innovating there can open pathways for global innovation.
Test the local identity work against the same brand ideals used at home, particularly coherence and differentiation.
caveats: The source gives directional guidance about market entry, not a step-by-step launch process or cost estimate.
Dialect and naming assessments require local expert and legal review; this card does not replace that.

Authenticity Authenticity is not possible without an organization having clarity about its market, positioning, value proposition, and competitive difference. Differentiation Brands always compete with each other within their business category, and at some level, compete with all brands that want our attention, our loyalty, and our money. Tait Vice President System Communications and Marketing Spectrum Health System Spectrum Health System’s mosaic represents the many parts of the organization working together to form a unified, integrated health system. Plato First Alcibiades In psychology, authenticity refers to self-knowledge and making decisions that are congruent with that self-knowledge. Organizations who know who they are, and what they stand for, start the identity process from a position of strength. They create brands that are sustainable and genuine.
